advance_directive_name: Advance Directive for Health Care (living will and health care proxy combined)
advance_directive_requirements: The form is set out in Ala. Code § 22-8A-4. It must be in writing, signed and dated, and witnessed by two people age 19 or older; no notary is required.
hospice_refusal: An adult age 19 or older who is alert and mentally capable may refuse any medical procedure or treatment, including life-saving and life-sustaining treatment and artificially provided food and liquids. Hospice care focuses on comfort and pain relief, and a person may stop curative treatment.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Alabama. The Assisted Suicide Ban Act, Ala. Code §§ 22-8B-1 to 22-8B-7 (2017), makes it a Class C felony for a physician or health care provider to prescribe a drug or perform a procedure deliberately to aid in dying.
notes: The prohibiting statute cite (Ala. Code §§ 22-8B-1 to 22-8B-7) comes from a secondary summary of the 2017 act; the Alabama Medicaid advance-directive page is the official source for the form.
polst_note: Alabama has no statewide POLST program or statutory POLST form; do-not-resuscitate orders are handled separately by a physician.
proxy_how: Name a competent adult in Part 2 of the Advance Directive for Health Care under Ala. Code § 22-8A-4. The proxy decides on providing, withholding, or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment and artificially provided nutrition and hydration when the person is terminally ill or permanently unconscious, and only as the directive authorizes.

advance_directive_requirements: Under AS 13.52.010, the directive must be in writing, contain the date of its execution, be signed by the principal, and be witnessed as specified in that section.
hospice_refusal: An adult may give individual instructions, oral or written, refusing treatment under AS 13.52.010, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort. A health care agent or surrogate may make decisions if the person lacks capacity.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Alaska. The only bill considered, HB 54 (2017-2018, the Alaska Voluntary Termination of Life by Terminally Ill Individuals Act), passed one committee and died without becoming law.
notes: No official Alaska page with a downloadable POLST form was returned, so polst_url is null. The toll-free referral number 1-800-770-9999 also appears on the Alaska Bar site but the Anchorage number above was used.
polst_note: Alaska recognizes a statewide POLST under AS 13.52; since 2022 (HB 392) advanced practice registered nurses and physician assistants may also sign it. The form is completed with a health care provider and does not replace an advance health care directive.
proxy_how: Execute a durable power of attorney for health care under AS 13.52.010(b). The agent may make any health care decision the principal could have made while having capacity, and must follow the principal's instructions and known wishes.
proxy_name: Durable power of attorney for health care (health care agent)

advance_directive_name: Life Care Planning packet (Health Care Power of Attorney and Living Will)
advance_directive_requirements: Sign and date the form in front of at least one adult witness or a notary public under A.R.S. § 36-3221. The witness or notary may not be the agent or a person directly involved in the signer's health care at the time.
hospice_refusal: An adult may refuse medical treatment in a living will or through a health care agent, including life-sustaining treatment when terminally ill or permanently unconscious. Hospice care provides comfort care, and a person may decline curative treatment.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Arizona. Assisting a suicide is treated as manslaughter under A.R.S. § 13-1103, with no exception for physicians or terminal illness.
notes: The State Bar of Arizona does not run a traditional phone lawyer-referral service; its public page links to Find-a-Lawyer and low-cost programs, so no referral phone is listed.
polst_name: POLST (Portable Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: A POLST is a provider-signed medical order for a person who is seriously ill or frail. A blank POLST form is available through the Attorney General's Life Care Planning materials, and it is completed with a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner.
proxy_how: Name an adult agent in the Health Care Power of Attorney form (A.R.S. §§ 36-3221 et seq.). The agent makes health care decisions, including decisions about life-sustaining treatment, when the person cannot make or communicate them.
proxy_name: Health care agent (Health Care Power of Attorney)

advance_directive_name: Advance Care Plan Form and Appointment of Health Care Agent Form
advance_directive_requirements: A written advance directive must be either notarized or witnessed by two competent adult witnesses under the Arkansas Health Care Decisions Act.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may state in a declaration (living will) whether life-sustaining treatment should be withheld or withdrawn if terminally ill or permanently unconscious, once two physicians make that determination. Hospice care focuses on comfort, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Arkansas. A bill to authorize it, HB 1536 (the Compassionate Care End-of-Life Option Act, 2019), died in committee and was never enacted.
notes: No specific Arkansas statute criminalizing assisted suicide was verified from an official source, so maid_law is null. The living will is governed by the Arkansas Rights of the Terminally Ill or Permanently Unconscious Act.
polst_name: AR POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment)
polst_note: The Arkansas Department of Health prescribes the standardized pink POLST form under Act 504 of 2017. It is signed by the patient's physician and by the patient or legal representative, and it complements but does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent using the Appointment of Health Care Agent Form from the Arkansas Department of Health. The agent makes health care decisions for the person when the person lacks capacity, following the person's instructions and wishes.

hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop any medical treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort and pain relief. An advance health care directive or agent carries out those wishes if the person cannot communicate.
maid_eligibility: An adult age 18 or older with capacity to make medical decisions who has a terminal disease, meaning an incurable and irreversible disease that will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months.
maid_law: California End of Life Option Act, Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 443-443.22
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests to the attending physician at least 48 hours apart and one written request, confirmed by a consulting physician. Only the person may make the request and self-administer the drug; no one may request it on their behalf, including through an advance directive, and the person may rescind at any time.
notes: No official California page with a downloadable Advance Health Care Directive form was returned, so advance_directive_url and its witness requirements are null. The 48-hour interval reflects SB 380 (effective January 1, 2022), which shortened the original 15-day interval; the Act's sunset was set for January 1, 2031, with a 2025 bill (SB 403) proposed to repeal it.
polst_note: POLST is a standardized, immediately actionable physician order under Cal. Prob. Code §§ 4780-4785 for a person who is frail or elderly, has a compromised condition, or has a terminal illness. It supplements but does not replace an advance health care directive, and the official form is available at capolst.org.
proxy_how: Name an agent in an Advance Health Care Directive under Cal. Prob. Code Division 4.7. The agent makes health care decisions when the person is unable to make or communicate them, following the person's instructions and wishes.
proxy_name: Health care agent (agent under an Advance Health Care Directive)

advance_directive_name: Medical Durable Power of Attorney (MDPOA) and living will (declaration as to medical treatment)
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may refuse or stop medical treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, through an advance directive or agent. Hospice care provides comfort-focused care, and a person may decline curative treatment.
maid_eligibility: An adult resident of Colorado age 18 or older who is mentally capable, can make and communicate an informed decision, and has a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less, confirmed by two physicians.
maid_law: Colorado End-of-Life Options Act, C.R.S. §§ 25-48-101 to 25-48-123 (enacted by Proposition 106, 2016)
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests at least 15 days apart and one written request witnessed by two people. Either physician must refer the person for a mental-health evaluation if capability is in doubt, and the person may rescind the request at any time and may choose not to use the medication.
notes: Colorado has no statewide lawyer-referral service; the Colorado Bar Association page states it does not make individual referrals and directs the public to its Find-a-Lawyer directory, so help_phone is null. Witness requirements for the MDPOA were not verified from an official source, so that field is null.
polst_name: MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: MOST is Colorado's version of POLST: a medical order for a seriously ill person that records preferences for CPR, artificial nutrition and hydration, and other life-sustaining treatments. It is completed with a health care provider and does not replace an advance directive.
proxy_how: Complete a Medical Durable Power of Attorney under C.R.S. §§ 15-14-503 to 15-14-509 naming a health care agent. The agent makes medical decisions for the person if the person becomes unable to speak for them. In Colorado no one, including a spouse or adult child, can automatically make medical decisions for another adult.
proxy_name: Health care agent (named in a Medical Durable Power of Attorney)

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (living will and appointment of health care representative, combined form available)
advance_directive_requirements: The directive must be signed by the declarant and witnessed by two witnesses; a notary public may also witness it, and an optional witnesses' affidavit is available. No lawyer is needed to complete the forms.
hospice_refusal: MOLST and the living will rest on the right to accept or refuse medical treatment, including treatments that might extend life. A person may refuse or stop treatment and choose hospice care focused on comfort.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Connecticut. Connecticut has no aid-in-dying law, and bills to create one have been introduced but not enacted.
notes: Connecticut has no statewide lawyer-referral service; referrals are handled by county bar associations, so no statewide referral phone is listed. No specific Connecticut statute criminalizing assisted suicide was verified from an official source, so maid_law is null.
polst_note: MOLST is a medical order authorized statewide by Public Act 17-70 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-580h) for a person approaching the end stage of a serious, life-limiting illness or in advanced chronic progressive frailty. It is voluntary, is not an advance directive, and is completed with a clinician.
proxy_how: Appoint a health care representative in writing under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-575a. The representative may make any and all health care decisions on the person's behalf, including whether to withhold or withdraw life support, when the person is unable to make or communicate decisions.

advance_directive_name: Advance Health Care Directive (health-care instruction and power of attorney for health care)
advance_directive_requirements: Under the rewritten 16 Del. C. ch. 25, a health-care instruction requires no signature, witness, or writing, while a power of attorney for health care must be a signed record witnessed by one adult witness.
hospice_refusal: An adult with decision-making capacity may plan ahead through an advance health care directive or a DMOST form and have those wishes respected, including refusing life-sustaining treatment. Hospice care provides comfort care, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_eligibility: An adult resident of Delaware with a terminal illness and a prognosis of six months or less to live, who has decision-making capacity, is making an informed decision, and is acting voluntarily, as confirmed by both an attending physician or APRN and a consulting physician or APRN.
maid_law: The Ron Silverio/Heather Block End of Life Options Law, 16 Del. C. ch. 25C (House Bill 140, signed May 20, 2025)
maid_safeguards: The person must make two oral requests and one written request; the second oral request must come at least 15 days after the first, and the written request must be signed by two adult witnesses. Only the person may request the medication, not a guardian, surrogate, or agent, and the person may rescind at any time. Providers must report prescriptions to the Department of Health and Social Services.
notes: The End of Life Options Law takes effect when final regulations are promulgated or January 1, 2026, whichever occurs first. Delaware rewrote its advance-directive chapter (84 Del. Laws ch. 467), effective September 30, 2025, so older two-witness descriptions are outdated. A 2026 bill (SB 274) proposes renaming DMOST to POLST. No official Delaware page with a downloadable advance-directive form was returned, so advance_directive_url is null. The Bar states it cannot recommend an attorney by phone; referrals go through the online Legal Help Link.
polst_name: DMOST (Delaware Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment)
polst_note: DMOST is a portable medical order under 16 Del. C. ch. 25A for a patient with serious illness or frailty whose practitioner would not be surprised if they died within the next year. It must be signed by the patient or authorized representative and a physician, APRN, or physician assistant, and it is separate from an advance health care directive.
proxy_how: Name an agent in a power of attorney for health care under 16 Del. C. § 2508. The agent makes health care decisions when the person is found to lack capacity, following the person's instructions and wishes.
proxy_name: Agent (under a power of attorney for health care)

advance_directive_requirements: Under Fla. Stat. § 765.302, a living will must be signed by the principal in the presence of two subscribing witnesses, one of whom is neither a spouse nor a blood relative of the principal.
hospice_refusal: A competent adult may direct in a living will that life-prolonging procedures be withheld or withdrawn if terminally ill, in an end-stage condition, or in a persistent vegetative state, and may choose hospice care focused on comfort and pain relief.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Florida. Fla. Stat. § 782.08 makes deliberately assisting another person's self-murder manslaughter, a second-degree felony punishable by up to 15 years in prison, with no exception for physicians or terminal illness. Fla. Stat. § 765.309 states that the advance-directives chapter does not authorize mercy killing or euthanasia.
notes: A 2025 bill (SB 1700, Florida End-of-Life Options Act) and a prefiled 2026 bill (SB 312) would have authorized aid in dying but were not enacted.
polst_name: POLST — no statewide statutory form; DNRO (Do Not Resuscitate Order, DH Form 1896) used instead
polst_note: Florida has no statewide POLST form in statute. The Department of Health's DNRO (DH Form 1896) is a one-page order, printed on yellow paper and signed by the patient's physician or other authorized provider, directing paramedics and EMTs not to resuscitate. POLST-type orders may also be used in hospitals, facilities, and hospice.
proxy_how: Designate a competent adult as health care surrogate in writing under Fla. Stat. § 765.202. The surrogate makes health care decisions and receives health information needed for those decisions when the principal is incapacitated.

advance_directive_name: Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care
advance_directive_requirements: The person must be 18 or older or an emancipated minor and of sound mind, and must sign the form with two witnesses.
hospice_refusal: A person may use the Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care to accept or refuse life-sustaining procedures and artificial nutrition or hydration when terminally ill or permanently unconscious, once the condition is certified in writing. Hospice care provides comfort care, and treatment may be refused or stopped.
maid_prohibited_note: Medical aid in dying is not authorized in Georgia. O.C.G.A. § 16-5-5 makes it a felony, punishable by 1 to 10 years in prison, for a person with actual knowledge that someone intends suicide to knowingly and willfully assist in that suicide. The statute does not apply to pain-relief care or to withholding or withdrawing treatment under an advance directive.
notes: The Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care (O.C.G.A. Title 31, Chapter 32) replaced the separate living will and durable power of attorney for health care on July 1, 2007. The State Bar of Georgia states it cannot refer an attorney and directs people to local and voluntary bar associations, so no referral phone is listed.
polst_note: Georgia's POLST is a medical order under O.C.G.A. § 31-1-14 for a patient with a serious illness who is expected to die within 365 days, or with dementia or another progressive degenerative brain condition. It is completed with the attending physician and signed by the patient or an authorized person and the physician.
proxy_how: Name a health care agent in Part 1 of the Georgia Advance Directive for Health Care under O.C.G.A. § 31-32-8. The agent carries out the person's health care decisions when the person cannot, but may not consent to psychosurgery, sterilization, or involuntary hospitalization or treatment.
